BEL-IMPERIA at a window [above].

BEL-IMPERIA

1What means this outrage that is offer’d me?
2Why am I thus sequester’d from the court?
3No notice! Shall I not know the cause
4Of these my secret and suspicious ills?
5Accursèd brother, unkind murderer,
6Why bends thou thus thy mind to martyr me?
7Hieronimo, why writ I of thy wrongs,
8Or why art thou so slack in thy revenge?
9Andrea, O Andrea! that thou saw’st
10Me for thy friend Horatio handled thus,
11And him for me thus causeless murdered! —
12Well, force perforce, I must constrain myself
13To patience, and apply me to the time,
14Till heav’n, as I have hop’d, shall set me free.

Enter CHRISTOPHIL

15Come, madam Bel-imperia, this may not be.

Exeunt.

[SCENE X]

Enter LORENZO, BALTHAZAR, and the PAGE.

LORENZO

1Boy, talk no further; thus far things go well.
2Thou art assurèd that thou saw’st him dead?

PAGE

3Or else, my lord, I live not.

LORENZO

Or else, my lord, I live not. That’s enough.
4As for his resolution in his end,
5Leave that to him with whom he sojourns now.
6Here, take my ring, and give it Christophil;
7And bid him let my sister be enlarg’d,
8And bring her hither straight. —

Exit Page.

9This that I did was for a policy,
10To smooth and keep the murder secret,
11Which, as a nine-days’ wonder, being o’erblown,
12My gentle sister will I now enlarge.

BALTHAZAR

13And time, Lorenzo: for my lord the duke,
14You heard, enquirèd for her yester-night.

LORENZO

15Why, and my lord, I hope you heard me say
16Sufficient reason why she kept away;
17But that’s all one. My lord, you love her?

BALTHAZAR

But that’s all one. My lord, you love her? Ay.

LORENZO

18Then in your love beware; deal cunningly:
19Salve all suspicions, only soothe me up;
20And if she hap to stand on terms with us,
21As for her sweetheart and concealment so,
22Jest with her gently; under feigned jest
23Are things conceal’d that else would breed unrest. —
24But here she comes.

Enter BEL-IMPERIA.

But here she comes. Now, sister!

BEL-IMPERIA

But here she comes. Now, sister! Sister? —No!
25Thou art no brother, but an enemy;
26Else wouldst thou not have us’d thy sister so:
27First, to affright me with thy weapons drawn,
28And with extremes abuse my company;
29And then to hurry me like whirlwind’s rage
30Amidst a crew of thy confederates,
31And clap me up, where none might come at me,
32Nor I at any to reveal my wrongs.
33What madding fury did possess thy wits?
34Or wherein is’t that I offended thee?

LORENZO

35Advise you better, Bel-imperia,
36For I have done you no disparagement;
37Unless, by more discretion than deserv’d,
38I sought to save your honour and mine own.

BEL-IMPERIA

39Mine honour? why, Lorenzo, wherein is’t
40That I neglect my reputation so,
41As you, or any, need to rescue it?

LORENZO

42His highness and my father were resolv’d
43To come confer with old Hieronimo,
44Concerning certain matters of estate,
45That by the Viceroy was determinèd.

BEL-IMPERIA

46And wherein was mine honour touch’d in that?

BALTHAZAR

47Have patience, Bel-imperia; hear the rest.

LORENZO

48Me (next in sight) as messenger they sent,
49To give him notice that they were so nigh:
50Now when I came, consorted with the prince,
51And, unexpected in an arbour there,
52Found Bel-imperia with Horatio —

BEL-IMPERIA

53How then?

LORENZO

54Why, then, remembering that old disgrace,
55Which you for Don Andrea had endur’d,
56And now were likely longer to sustain,
57By being found so meanly accompanied,
58Thought rather —for I knew no readier mean —
59To thrust Horatio forth my father’s way.

BALTHAZAR

60And carry you obscurely somewhere else,
61Lest that his highness should have found you there.

BEL-IMPERIA

62Ev’n so, my lord? And you are witness
63That this is true which he entreateth of?
64You, gentle brother, forg’d this for my sake,
65And you, my lord, were made his instrument?
66A work of worth, worthy the noting too!
67But what’s the cause that you conceal’d me since?

LORENZO

68Your melancholy, sister, since the news
69Of your first favourite Don Andrea’s death,
70My father’s old wrath hath exasperate.

BALTHAZAR

71And better was’t for you, being in disgrace,
72To absent yourself and give his fury place.

BEL-IMPERIA

73But why had I no notice of his ire?

LORENZO

74That were to add more fuel to your fire,
75Who burnt like Aetna for Andrea’s loss.

BEL-IMPERIA

76Hath not my father then enquir’d for me?

LORENZO

77Sister, he hath, and thus excus’d I thee.

He whispereth in her ear.

78But, Bel-imperia, see the gentle Prince;
79Look on thy love, behold young Balthazar,
80Whose passions by thy presence are increas’d,
81And in whose melancholy thou may’st see
82Thy hate, his love; thy flight, his following thee.

BEL-IMPERIA

83Brother, you are become an orator —
84I know not, I, by what experience —
85Too politic for me, past all compare,
86Since last I saw you; but content yourself:
87The prince is meditating higher things.

BALTHAZAR

88’Tis of thy beauty then that conquers kings;
89Of those thy tresses, Ariadne’s twines,
90Wherewith my liberty thou hast surpris’d;
91Of that thine ivory front, my sorrow’s map,
92Wherein I see no haven to rest my hope.

BEL-IMPERIA

93To love and fear, and both at once, my lord,
94In my conceit, are things of more import
95Than women’s wits are to be busied with.

BALTHAZAR

96’Tis I that love.

BEL-IMPERIA

’Tis I that love. Whom?

BALTHAZAR

’Tis I that love. Whom? Bel-imperia.

BEL-IMPERIA

97But I that fear.

BALTHAZAR

But I that fear. Whom?

BEL-IMPERIA

But I that fear. Whom? Bel-imperia.

LORENZO

98Fear [you] yourself?

BEL-IMPERIA

Fear [you] yourself? Ay, brother.

LORENZO

Fear [you] yourself? Ay, brother. How?

BEL-IMPERIA

Fear [you] yourself? Ay, brother. How? As those
99That, what they love, are loath and fear to lose.

BALTHAZAR

100Then, fair, let Balthazar your keeper be.

BEL-IMPERIA

101No, Balthazar doth fear as well as we:
102Et tremulo metui pavidum iunxere timorem,
103Et vanum stolidae proditionis opus.

LORENZO

104Nay, an you argue things so cunningly,
105We’ll go continue this discourse at court.

BALTHAZAR

106Led by the lodestar of her heavenly looks,
107Wends poor, oppressèd Balthazar,
108As o’er the mountains walks the wanderer,
109Incertain to effect his pilgrimage.

Exeunt.

[SCENE XI]

Enter two PORTINGALES, and HIERONIMO meets them.

1 PORTINGALE

1By your leave, sir.

HIERONIMO

2<sup> Q4 </sup> ’Tis neither as you think, nor as you think,
3Nor as you think; you’re wide all:
4These slippers are not mine, they were my son Horatio’s.
5My son! and what’s a son? A thing begot
6Within a pair of minutes, thereabout;
7A lump bred up in darkness, and doth serve
8To ballace these light creatures we call women;
9And, at nine moneths’ end, creeps forth to light.
10What is there yet in a son,
11To make a father dote, rave, or run mad?
12Being born, it pouts, cries, and breeds teeth.
13What is there yet in a son? He must be fed,
14Be taught to go, and speak. Ay, or yet?
15Why might not a man love a calf as well?
16Or melt in passion o’er a frisking kid,
17As for a son? Methinks, a young bacon,
18Or a fine little smooth horse colt,
19Should move a man as much as doth a son:
20For one of these, in very little time,
21Will grow to some good use; whereas a son,
22The more he grows in stature and in years,
23The more unsquar’d, unbevell’d, he appears,
24Reckons his parents among the rank of fools,
25Strikes care upon their heads with his mad riots;
26Makes them look old, before they meet with age.
27This is a son! —And what a loss were this,
28Consider’d truly? —O, but my Horatio
29Grew out of reach of these insatiate humours:
30He lov’d his loving parents;
31He was my comfort, and his mother’s joy,
32The very arm that did hold up our house:
33Our hopes were storèd up in him,
34None but a damnèd murderer could hate him.
35He had not seen the back of nineteen year,
36When his strong arm unhors’d the proud Prince Balthazar,
37and his great mind,
38Too full of honour, took him unto mercy —
39That valiant, but ignoble Portugal!
40Well, heaven is heaven still!
41And there is Nemesis, and Furies,
42And things call’d whips,
43And they sometimes do meet with murderers:
44They do not always ’scape, that’s some comfort.
45Ay, ay, ay; and then time steals on,
46And steals, and steals till violence leaps forth
47Like thunder wrapp’d in a ball of fire,
48And so doth bring confusion to them all.] </sup> Q4 <sup>
49Good leave have you: nay, I pray you go,
50For I’ll leave you, if you can leave me so.

2 PORTINGALE

51Pray you, which is the next way to my lord the duke’s?

HIERONIMO

52The next way from me.

1 PORTINGALE

The next way from me. To his house, we mean.

HIERONIMO

53Oh, hard by; ’tis yon house that you see.

2 PORTINGALE

54You could not tell us if his son were there?

HIERONIMO

55Who, my lord Lorenzo?

1 PORTINGALE

Who, my lord Lorenzo? Ay, sir.

He goeth in at one door and comes out at another.

HIERONIMO

Who, my lord Lorenzo? Ay, sir. Oh, forbear!
56For other talk for us far fitter were.
57But if you be importunate to know
58The way to him and where to find him out,
59Then list to me, and I’ll resolve your doubt.
60There is a path upon your left-hand side,
61That leadeth from a guilty conscience
62Unto a forest of distrust and fear,
63A darksome place, and dangerous to pass;
64There shall you meet with melancholy thoughts,
65Whose baleful humours if you but uphold,
66It will conduct you to Despair and Death;
67Whose rocky cliffs when you have once beheld,
68Within a hugy dale of lasting night,
69That, kindl’d with the world’s iniquities,
70Doth cast up filthy and detested fumes,
71Not far from thence, where murderers have built
72A habitation for their cursèd souls,
73There, in a brazen cauldron fix’d by Jove
74In his fell wrath upon a sulphur flame,
75Yourselves shall find Lorenzo bathing him
76In boiling lead and blood of innocents.

1 PORTUGAL

77Ha, ha, ha!

HIERONIMO

78Ha, ha, ha!
79Why, ha, ha, ha! Farewell, good ha, ha, ha!

Exit.

2 PORTUGAL

80Doubtless this man is passing lunatic,
81Or imperfection of his age doth make him dote.
82Come, let’s away to seek my lord the duke.

Exeunt.

[SCENE XII]

Enter HIERONIMO, with a poniard in one hand and a rope in the other.

HIERONIMO

1Now, sir, perhaps I come and see the King;
2The King sees me, and fain would hear my suit:
3Why, is not this a strange and seld-seen thing,
4That standers-by with toys should strike me mute?
5Go to, I see their shifts, and say no more.
6Hieronimo, ’tis time for thee to trudge:
7Down by the dale that flows with purple gore,
8Standeth a fiery tower; There sits a judge
9Upon a seat of steel and molten brass,
10And ’twixt his teeth he holds a fire-brand,
11That leads unto the lake where hell doth stand.
12Away, Hieronimo! to him be gone:
13He’ll do thee justice for Horatio’s death.
14Turn down this path, thou shalt be with him straight;
15Or this, and then thou need’st not take thy breath:
16This way, or that way! —Soft and fair, not so:
17For if I hang or kill myself, let’s know
18Who will revenge Horatio’s murder then?
19No, no, fie, no. Pardon me, I’ll none of that.
20He flings away the dagger and halter.
21This way I’ll take, and this way comes the King:
22He takes them up again.
23And here I’ll have a fling at him, that’s flat:
24And, Balthazar, I’ll be with thee to bring,
25And thee, Lorenzo! Here’s the King —nay, stay;
26And here, ay, here —there goes the hare away.

Enter KING, AMBASSADOR, CASTILE, and LORENZO.

KING

27Now show, Ambassador, what our Viceroy saith:
28Hath he receiv’d the articles we sent?

HIERONIMO

29Justice, O, justice to Hieronimo!

LORENZO

30Back! See’st thou not the King is busy?

HIERONIMO

31Oh, is he so?

KING

32Who is he that interrupts our business?

HIERONIMO

33Not I. Hieronimo, beware! go by, go by!

AMBASSADOR

34Renownèd King, he hath receiv’d and read
35Thy kingly proffers and thy promised league;
36And, as a man extremely overjoy’d
37To hear his son so princely entertain’d,
38Whose death he had so solemnly bewail’d,
39This for thy further satisfaction
40And kingly love, he kindly lets thee know:
41First, for the marriage of his princely son
42With Bel-imperia, thy belovèd niece,
43The news are more delightful to his soul,
44Than myrrh or incense to the offended heavens.
45In person, therefore, will he come himself,
46To see the marriage rites solemnisèd,
47And, in the presence of the court of Spain,
48To knit a sure inexplicable band
49Of kingly love and everlasting league
50Betwixt the crowns of Spain and Portingale.
51There will he give his crown to Balthazar,
52And make a queen of Bel-imperia.

KING

53Brother, how like you this our Viceroy’s love?

CASTILE

54No doubt, my lord, it is an argument
55Of honourable care to keep his friend,
56And wondrous zeal to Balthazar his son;
57Nor am I least indebted to his grace,
58That bends his liking to my daughter thus.

AMBASSADOR

59Now last, dread lord, here hath his highness sent
60(Although he send not that his son return)
61His ransom due to Don Horatio.

HIERONIMO

62Horatio! who calls Horatio?

KING

63And well remember’d: Thank his majesty.
64Here, see it given to Horatio.

HIERONIMO

65Justice, O, justice, justice, gentle King!

KING

66Who is that? Hieronimo?

HIERONIMO

67Justice, O, justice! O my son, my son!
68My son, whom naught can ransom or redeem!

LORENZO

69Hieronimo, you are not well-advis’d.

HIERONIMO

70Away, Lorenzo, hinder me no more;
71For thou hast made me bankrupt of my bliss.
72Give me my son! you shall not ransom him!
73Away! I’ll rip the bowels of the earth,

He diggeth with his dagger

74And ferry over to th’Elysian plains,
75And bring my son to show his deadly wounds.
76Stand from about me!
77I’ll make a pickaxe of my poniard,
78And here surrender up my marshalship;
79For I’ll go marshal up the fiends in hell
80To be avengèd on you all for this.

KING

81What means this outrage?
82Will none of you restrain his fury?

HIERONIMO

83Nay, soft and fair! you shall not need to strive:
84Needs must he go that the devils drive.

Exit.

KING

85What accident hath happ’d Hieronimo?
86I have not seen him to demean him so.

LORENZO

87My gracious lord, he is with extreme pride,
88Conceiv’d of young Horatio his son,
89And covetous of having to himself
90The ransom of the young Prince Balthazar,
91Distract and in a manner lunatic.

KING

92Believe me, nephew, we are sorry for’t:
93This is the love that fathers bear their sons.
94But, gentle brother, go give to him this gold,
95The Prince’s ransom; let him have his due.
96For what he hath, Horatio shall not want;
97Haply Hieronimo hath need thereof.

LORENZO

98But if he be thus helplessly distract,
99’Tis requisite his office be resign’d
100And given to one of more discretion.

KING

101We shall increase his melancholy so.
102’Tis best that we see further in it first,
103Till when ourself will not exempt the place.
104And, brother, now bring in the Ambassador,
105That he may be a witness of the match
106’Twixt Balthazar and Bel-imperia,
107And that we may prefix a certain time,
108Wherein the marriage shall be solemnis’d,
109That we may have thy lord the Viceroy, here.

AMBASSADOR

110Therein your highness highly shall content
111His majesty, that longs to hear from hence.

KING

112On, then, and hear you, Lord Ambassador. —

Exeunt.

<sup> Q4 </sup> [SCENE XIIA]

Enter JAQUES and PEDRO.

JAQUES

1I wonder, Pedro, why our master thus
2At midnight sends us with our torches light,
3When man, and bird, and beast, are all at rest,
4Save those that watch for rape and bloody murder?

PEDRO

5O Jaques, know thou that our master’s mind
6Is much distraught, since his Horatio died,
7And — now his agèd years should sleep in rest,
8His heart in quiet — like a desperate man,
9Grows lunatic and childish for his son.
10Sometimes, as he doth at his table sit,
11He speaks as if Horatio stood by him;
12Then starting in a rage, falls on the earth,
13Cries out ‘Horatio, where is my Horatio?’
14So that with extreme grief and cutting sorrow
15There is not left in him one inch of man:
16See, where he comes.

Enter HIERONIMO.

HIERONIMO

17I pry through every crevice of each wall,
18Look on each tree, and search through every brake,
19Beat at the bushes, stamp our grandam earth,
20Dive in the water, and stare up to heaven:
21Yet cannot I behold my son Horatio. —
22How now, who’s there? Sprits, sprits?

PEDRO

23We are your servants that attend you, sir.

HIERONIMO

24What make you with your torches in the dark?

PEDRO

25You bid us light them and attend you here.

HIERONIMO

26No, no, you are deceiv‘d, not I, —you are deceiv’d!
27Was I so mad to bid you light your torches now?
28Light me your torches at the mid of noon,
29Whenas the sun-god rides in all his glory;
30Light me your torches then.

PEDRO

Light me your torches then. Then we burn daylight.

HIERONIMO

31Let it be burnt; Night is a murd‘rous slut,
32That would not have her treasons to be seen;
33And yonder pale-fac‘d Hecate there, the moon,
34Doth give consent to that is done in darkness,
35And all those stars that gaze upon her face,
36Are aglets on her sleeve, pins on her train;
37And those that should be powerful and divine,
38Do sleep in darkness, when they most should shine.

PEDRO

39Provoke them not, fair sir, with tempting words:
40The heav‘ns are gracious, and your miseries
41And sorrow makes you speak you know not what.

HIERONIMO

42Villain, thou liest, and thou doest naught
43But tell me I am mad: thou liest, I am not mad!
44I know thee to be Pedro, and he Jaques.
45I’ll prove it to thee; and were I mad, how could I?
46Where was she that same night when my Horatio
47Was murder‘d?
48She should have shone: Search thou the book.
49Had the moon shone
50In my boy’s face there was a kind of grace,
51That I know —nay, I do know—had the murderer seen him,
52His weapon would have fall‘n and cut the earth,
53Had he been fram‘d of naught but blood and death.
54Alack! when mischief doth it knows not what,
55What shall we say to mischief?

Enter ISABELLA.

ISABELLA

56Dear Hieronimo, come in a-doors;
57O, seek not means so to increase thy sorrow.

HIERONIMO

58Indeed, Isabella, we do nothing here:
59I do not cry: ask Pedro, and ask Jaques;
60Not I, indeed; we are very merry, very merry.

ISABELLA

61How? be merry here, be merry here?
62Is not this the place, and this the very tree,
63Where my Horatio died, where he was murder‘d?

HIERONIMO

64Was — do not say what: Let her weep it out.
65This was the tree; I set it of a kernel:
66And when our hot Spain could not let it grow,
67But that the infant and the human sap
68Began to wither, duly twice a morning
69Would I be sprinkling it with fountain-water.
70At last it grew and grew, and bore and bore,
71Till at the length
72It grew a gallows, and did bear our son:
73It bore thy fruit and mine —O wicked, wicked plant!

One knocks within at the door.

74See who knock there.

PEDRO

See who knock there. It is a painter, sir.

HIERONIMO

75Bid him come in, and paint some comfort,
76For surely there’s none lives but painted comfort.
77Let him come in! —One knows not what may chance:
78God’s will that I should set this tree! —But even so
79Masters ungrateful servants rear from naught,
80And then they hate them that did bring them up.

Enter the PAINTER.

PAINTER

81God bless you, sir.

HIERONIMO

God bless you, sir. Wherefore? why, thou scornful villain?
82How, where, or by what means should I be bless‘d?

ISABELLA

83What wouldst thou have, good fellow?

PAINTER

What wouldst thou have, good fellow? Justice, madam.

HIERONIMO

84O ambitious beggar!
85Wouldst thou have that that lives not in the world?
86Why, all the undelv‘d mines cannot buy
87An ounce of justice. ’tis a jewel so inestimable.
88I tell thee,
89God hath engross‘d all justice in his hands,
90And there is none but what comes from him.

PAINTER

91Oh, then I see
92That God must right me for my murder‘d son.

HIERONIMO

93How, was thy son murder‘d?

PAINTER

94Ay, sir; no man did hold a son so dear.

HIERONIMO

95What, not as thine? That’s a lie,
96As massy as the earth: I had a son,
97Whose least unvalu‘d hair did weigh
98A thousand of thy son’s: and he was murder‘d.

PAINTER

99Alas, sir, I had no more but he.

HIERONIMO

100Nor I, nor I: but this same one of mine
101Was worth a legion. But all is one.
102Pedro, Jaques, go in a-doors; Isabella, go,
103And this good fellow here and I
104Will range this hideous orchard up and down,
105Like to two lions reavèd of their young.
106Go in a-doors, I say.

Exeunt. The Painter and he sits down

Go in a-doors, I say. Come, let’s talk wisely now.
107Was thy son murder‘d?

PAINTER

Was thy son murder‘d? Ay, sir.

HIERONIMO

Was thy son murder‘d? Ay, sir. So was mine.
108How dost take it? art thou not sometimes mad?
109Is there no tricks that comes before thine eyes?

PAINTER

110O Lord, yes, sir.

HIERONIMO

Art a painter? Canst paint me a tear, or a wound, a groan,
or a sigh? Canst paint me such a tree as this?

PAINTER

Sir, I am sure you have heard of my painting: My name’s
Bazardo.

HIERONIMO

Bazardo! afore God, an excellent fellow. Look you, sir,
do you see, I’d have youpaint me in my gallery, in your
oil-colours, matted, and draw me five years younger than I
am —do ye see, sir, let five years go; let them go — like
the Marshal of Spain. My wife Isabella standing by me, with
a speaking look to my son Horatio, which should intend to
this or some such-like purpose: God bless thee, my sweet
son;’ and my hand leaning upon his head, thus, sir; do you
see? —May it be done?

PAINTER

Very well, sir.

HIERONIMO

Nay, I pray, mark me, sir: then, sir, would I have you
paint me this tree, this very tree. Canst paint a doleful cry?

PAINTER

Seemingly, sir.

HIERONIMO

Nay, it should cry: but all is one. Well, sir, paint me a
youth run through and through with villains’ swords, hanging
upon this tree. Canst thou draw a murderer?

PAINTER

I’ll warrant you, sir, I have the pattern of the most notorious villains that ever lived in all Spain.

HIERONIMO

O, let them be worse, worse; stretch thine art, and let their
beards be of Judas his own colour; and let their eye-brows
jutty over: in any case observe that. Then, sir, after some
violent noise, bring me forth in my shirt, and my gown under
mine arm, with my torch in my hand, and my sword reared up
thus: —and with these words:
‘What noise is this? Who calls Hieronimo?’
May it be done?

PAINTER

Yea, sir.

HIERONIMO

Well, sir; then bring me forth, bring me through alley and
alley, still with a distracted countenance going along, and let
my hair heave up my night-cap. Let the clouds scowl, make
the moon dark, the stars extinct, the winds blowing, the bells
tolling, the owl shrieking, the toads croaking, the minutes
jarring, an the clock striking twelve. And then at last, sir,
starting, behold a man hanging, and tottering, and tottering, as
you know the wind will wave a man, and I with a trice to cut him
down. And looking upon him by the advantage of my torch, find
it to be my son Horatio. There you may show a passion, there
you may show a passion! Draw me like old Priam of Troy,
crying: ‘The house is afire, the house is afire, as the torch
over my head!‘ Make me curse, make me rave, make me cry,
make me mad, make me well again, make me curse hell,
invocate heaven, and in the end eave me in a trance —and so
forth.

PAINTER

And is this the end?

HIERONIMO

O no, there is no end: the end is death and madness! As
I am never better tan when I am mad, then methinks I am
a brave fellow, then I do wonders: but reason abuseth me,
and there’s the torment, there’s the hell. At the last, sir, bring
me to one of the murderers; were he as strong as Hector,
thus would I tear and drag him up and down.

He beats the Painter in, then comes out again,with a book in his hand. </sup> Q4 <sup>

[SCENE XIII]

Enter HIERONIMO with a book in his hand.

[HIERONIMO]

1Vindicta mihi!
2Ay, heaven will be reveng’d of every ill;
3Nor will they suffer murder unrepaid.
4Then stay, Hieronimo, attend their will:
5For mortal men may not appoint their time! —
6“Per scelus semper tutum est sceleribus iter.”
7Strike, and strike home, where wrong is offer’d thee;
8For evils unto ills conductors be,
9And death’s the worst of resolution.
10For he that thinks with patience to contend
11To quiet life, his life shall easily end. —
12“Fata si miseros iuvant, habes salutem;
13Fata si vitam negant, habes sepulchrum:”
14If destiny thy miseries do ease,
15Then hast thou health, and happy shalt thou be;
16If destiny deny thee life, Hieronimo,
17Yet shalt thou be assurèd of a tomb:
18If neither, yet let this thy comfort be:
19Heaven covereth him that hath no burial.
20And to conclude, I will revenge his death!
21But how? Not as the vulgar wits of men,
22With open but inevitable ills,
23As by a secret, yet a certain mean,
24Which under kindship will be cloakèd best.
25Wise men will take their opportunity
26Closely and safely fitting things to time.
27But in extremes advantage hath no time;
28And therefore all times fit not for revenge.
29Thus therefore will I rest me in unrest,
30Dissembling quiet in unquietness,
31Not seeming that I know their villainies,
32That my simplicity may make them think
33That ignorantly I will let all slip;
34For ignorance, I wot, and well they know,
35Remedium malorum iners est.
36Nor aught avails it me to menace them,
37Who, as a wintry storm upon a plain,
38Will bear me down with their nobility.
39No, no, Hieronimo, thou must enjoin
40Thine eyes to observation, and thy tongue
41To milder speeches than thy spirit affords,
42Thy heart to patience, and thy hands to rest,
43Thy cap to courtesy, and thy knee to bow,
44Till to revenge thou know, when, where and how.

A noise within.

45How now, what noise? What coil is that you keep?

Enter a SERVANT.

SERVANT

46Here are a sort of poor petitioners,
47That are importunate, an it shall please you, sir,
48That you should plead their cases to the King.

HIERONIMO

49That I should plead their several actions?
50Why, let them enter, and let me see them.

Enter three CITIZENS and an OLD MAN.

1 CITIZEN

51[to the other Citizens] So I tell you this: for learning and for law,
52There is not any advocate in Spain
53That can prevail, or will take half the pain
54That he will, in pursuit of equity.

HIERONIMO

55Come near, you men that thus importune me. —
56[Aside.] Now must I bear a face of gravity;aparte
57For thus I us’d before my marshalship,
58To plead in causes as corregidor. —
59Come on, sirs, what’s the matter?

2 CITIZEN

Come on, sirs, what’s the matter? Sir, an action.

HIERONIMO

60Of battery?

1 CITIZEN

Of battery? Mine of debt.

HIERONIMO

Of battery? Mine of debt. Give place.

2 CITIZEN

61No, sir, mine is an action of the case.

3 CITIZEN

62Mine an ejectione firmae by a lease.

HIERONIMO

63Content you, sirs; Are you determinèd
64That I should plead your several actions?

1 CITIZEN

65Ay, sir, and here’s my declaration.

2 CITIZEN

66And here is my bond.

3 CITIZEN

And here is my bond. And here is my lease.

They give him papers.

HIERONIMO

67But wherefore stands yon silly man so mute,
68With mournful eyes and hands to heav’n uprear’d?
69Come hither, father, let me know thy cause.

OLD MAN

70O worth y sir, my cause, but slightly known,
71May move the hearts of warlike Myrmidons,
72And melt the Corsic rocks with ruthful tears.

HIERONIMO

73Say, father, tell me, what’s thy suit?

OLD MAN

74No, sir, could my woes
75Give way unto my most distressful words,
76Then could I not in paper, as you see,
77With ink bewray what blood began in me.

HIERONIMO

78What’s here? ‘The humble supplication
79of Don Bazulto for his murder’d son.’

OLD MAN

80Ay, sir.

HIERONIMO

Ay, sir. No, sir, it was my murder’d son:
81Oh, my son, my son, oh, my son Horatio!
82But mine, or thine, Bazulto, be content.
83Here, take my handkercher, and wipe thine eyes,
84Whiles wretched I in thy mishaps may see
85The lively portrait of my dying self.

He draweth out a bloody napkin.

86O no, not this; Horatio, this was thine;
87And when I dy’d it in thy dearest blood,
88This was a token ’twixt thy soul and me,
89That of thy death revengèd I should be.
90But here, take this, and this —what, my purse? —
91Ay, this, and that, and all of them are thine;
92For all as one are our extremities.

1 CITIZEN

93O, see the kindness of Hieronimo!

2 CITIZEN

94This gentleness shows him a gentleman.

HIERONIMO

95See, see, O see thy shame, Hieronimo;
96See here a loving father to his son!
97Behold the sorrows and the sad laments,
98That he delivereth for his son’s decease!
99If love’s effects so strives in lesser things,
100If love enforce such moods in meaner wits,
101If love express such power in poor estates:
102Hieronimo, whenas a raging sea,
103Toss’d with the wind and tide, o’erturneth them,
104The upper billows’ course of waves to keep,
105Whilst lesser waters labour in the deep:
106Then sham’st thou not, Hieronimo, to neglect
107The sweet revenge of thy Horatio?
108Though on this earth justice will not be found,
109I’ll down to hell, and in this passion
110Knock at the dismal gates of Pluto’s court,
111Getting by force, as once Alcides did,
112A troop of Furies and tormenting hags
113To torture Don Lorenzo and the rest.
114Yet lest the triple-headed porter should
115Deny my passage to the slimy strand,
116The Thracian poet thou shalt counterfeit:
117Come on, old father, be my Orpheus,
118And if thou canst no notes upon the harp,
119Then sound the burden of thy sore heart’s grief,
120Till we do gain that Proserpine may grant
121Revenge on them that murderèd my son.
122Then will I rend and tear them thus and thus,
123Shiv’ring their limbs in pieces with my teeth.

Tears the papers.

1 CITIZEN

124O sir, my declaration!

Exit Hieronimo, and they after.

2 CITIZEN

O sir, my declaration! Save my bond!

Enter HIERONIMO

3 CITIZEN

125Alas, my lease! it cost me ten pound,
126And you, my lord, have torn the same.

HIERONIMO

127That cannot be, I gave it never a wound;
128Show me one drop of blood fall from the same:
129How is it possible I should slay it then?
130Tush, no; run after, catch me if you can.

Exeunt all but the old man. Bazulto remains till HIERONIMO enters again, who, staring him in the face, speaks.

HIERONIMO

131And art thou come, Horatio, from the depth,
132To ask for justice in this upper earth,
133To tell thy father thou art unreveng’d,
134To wring more tears from Isabella’s eyes,
135Whose lights are dimm’d with over-long laments?
136Go back, my son, complain to Aeacus,
137For here’s no justice; gentle boy, be gone,
138For justice is exilèd from the earth:
139Hieronimo will bear thee company.
140Thy mother cries on righteous Rhadamanth
141For just revenge against the murderers.

OLD MAN

142Alas, my lord, whence springs this troubled speech?

HIERONIMO

143But let me look on my Horatio.
144Sweet boy, how art thou chang’d in death’s black shade!
145Had Proserpine no pity on thy youth,
146But suffer’d thy fair crimson-colour’d spring
147With wither’d winter to be blasted thus?
148Horatio, thou art older than thy father:
149Ah, ruthless fate, that favour thus transforms!

OLD MAN

150Ah, my good lord, I am not your young son.

HIERONIMO

151What, not my son? Thou then a Fury art,
152Sent from the empty kingdom of black night
153To summon me to make appearance
154Before grim Minos and just Rhadamanth,
155To plague Hieronimo that is remiss,
156And seeks not vengeance for Horatio’s death.

OLD MAN

157I am a grievèd man, and not a ghost,
158That came for justice for my murder’d son.

HIERONIMO

159Ay, now I know thee, now thou nam’st thy son:
160Thou art the lively image of my grief;
161Within thy face, my sorrows I may see.
162Thy eyes are gumm’d with tears, thy cheeks are wan,
163Thy forehead troubled, and thy mutt’ring lips
164Murmur sad words abruptly broken off
165By force of windy sighs thy spirit breathes,
166And all this sorrow riseth for thy son:
167And selfsame sorrow feel I for my son.
168Come in, old man, thou shalt to Isabel;
169Lean on my arm; I thee, thou me shalt stay;
170And thou, and I, and she will sing a song,
171Three parts in one, but all of discords fram’d.
172Talk not of cords, but let us now be gone,
173For with a cord Horatio was slain.

Exeunt.

[SCENE XIV]

Enter KING of Spain, the Duke, VICEROY, and LORENZO, BALTHAZAR, DON PEDRO, and BEL-IMPERIA.

KING

1Go, brother, ‘tis the Duke of Castile’s cause;
2Salute the Viceroy in our name.

CASTILE

Salute the Viceroy in our name. I go.

VICEROY

3Go forth, Don Pedro, for thy nephew’s sake,
4And greet the Duke of Castile.

DON PEDRO

And greet the Duke of Castile. It shall be so.

KING

5And now to meet these Portuguese:
6For as we now are, so sometimes were these,
7Kings and commanders of the western Indies.
8Welcome, brave Viceroy, to the court of Spain,
9And welcome, all his honourable train!
10’Tis not unknown to us for why you come,
11Or have so kingly cross’d the seas:
12Sufficeth it, in this we note the troth,
13And more than common love you lend to us.
14So is it that mine honourable niece
15(For it beseems us now that it be known)
16Already is betroth’d to Balthazar:
17And by appointment and our condescent
18To-morrow are they to be marrièd.
19To this intent we entertain thyself,
20Thy followers, their pleasure, and our peace.
21Speak, men of Portingale, shall it be so?
22If ay, say so; if not, say flatly no.

VICEROY

23Renownèd King, I come not as thou think’st,
24With doubtful followers, unresolvèd men,
25But such as have upon thine articles
26Confirm’d thy motion and contented me.
27Know, sovereign, I come to solemnise
28The marriage of thy belovèd niece,
29Fair Bel-imperia, with my Balthazar,
30With thee, my son; whom sith I live to see,
31Here take my crown; I give it her and thee;
32And let me live a solitary life,
33In ceaseless prayers,
34To think how strangely heav’n hath thee preserv’d.

KING

35See, brother, see, how nature strives in him!
36Come, worthy Viceroy, and accompany
37Thy friend [, to strive] with thine extremities:
38A place more private fits this princely mood.

VICEROY

39Or here, or where your highness thinks it good.

Exeunt all but Castile and Lorenzo.

CASTILE

40Nay, stay, Lorenzo, let me talk with you.
41See’st thou this entertainment of these kings?

LORENZO

42I do, my lord, and joy to see the same.

CASTILE

43And know’st thou why this meeting is?

LORENZO

44For her, my lord, whom Balthazar doth love,
45And to confirm their promis’d marriage.

CASTILE

46She is thy sister?

LORENZO

She is thy sister? Who, Bel-imperia? Ay,
47My gracious lord, and this is the day,
48That I have longed so happily to see.

CASTILE

49Thou wouldst be loath that any fault of thine
50Should intercept her in her happiness?

LORENZO

51Heavens will not let Lorenzo err so much.

CASTILE

52Why then, Lorenzo, listen to my words:
53It is suspected, and reported too,
54That thou, Lorenzo, wrong’st Hieronimo,
55And in his suits towards his majesty
56Still keep’st him back, and seeks to cross his suit.

LORENZO

57That I, my lord —?

CASTILE

58I tell thee, son, myself have heard it said,
59When (to my sorrow) I have been asham’d
60To answer for thee. Though thou art my son.
61Lorenzo, know’st thou not the common love
62And kindness that Hieronimo hath won
63By his deserts within the court of Spain?
64Or see’st thou not the King my brother’s care
65In his behalf, and to procure his health?
66Lorenzo, shouldst thou thwart his passions,
67And he exclaim against thee to the King,
68What honour were’t in this assembly,
69Or what a scandal were’t among the Kings
70To hear Hieronimo exclaim on thee?
71Tell me —and look thou tell me truly too —
72Whence grows the ground of this report in court?

LORENZO

73My lord, it lies not in Lorenzo’s power
74To stop the vulgar, liberal of their tongues:
75A small advantage makes a water-breach,
76And no man lives that long contenteth all.

CASTILE

77Myself have seen thee busy to keep back
78Him and his supplications from the King.

LORENZO

79Yourself, my lord, hath seen his passions,
80That ill beseem’d the presence of a king:
81And, for I pitied him in his distress,
82I held him thence with kind and courteous words,
83As free from malice to Hieronimo
84As to my soul, my lord.

CASTILE

85Hieronimo, my son, mistakes thee then.

LORENZO

86My gracious father, believe me so he doth.
87But what’s a silly man, distract in mind,
88To think upon the murder of his son?
89Alas! how easy is it for him to err!
90But for his satisfaction and the world’s,
91’Twere good, my lord, that Hieronimo and I
92Were reconcil’d, if he misconster me.

CASTILE

93Lorenzo, thou hast said, it shall be so.
94Go one of you, and call Hieronimo.

Enter BALTHAZAR and BEL-IMPERIA.

BALTHAZAR

95Come, Bel-imperia, Balthazar’s content,
96My sorrow’s ease and sovereign of my bliss,
97Sith heaven hath ordained thee to be mine:
98Disperse those clouds and melancholy looks,
99And clear them up with those thy sun-bright eyes,
100Wherein my hope and heaven’s fair beauty lies.

BEL-IMPERIA

101My looks, my lord, are fitting for my love,
102Which, new begun, can show no brighter yet.

BALTHAZAR

103New-kindled flames should burn as morning sun.

BEL-IMPERIA

104But not too fast, lest heat and all be done.
105I see my lord my father.

BALTHAZAR

I see my lord my father. Truce, my love,
106I’ll go salute him.

CASTILE

I’ll go salute him. Welcome, Balthazar,
107Welcome, brave Prince, the pledge of Castile’s peace!
108And welcome, Bel-imperia! —How now, girl?
109Why com’st thou sadly to salute us thus?
110Content thyself, for I am satisfied:
111It is not now as when Andrea liv’d.
112We have forgotten and forgiven that,
113And thou art gracèd with a happier love. —
114But, Balthazar, here comes Hieronimo;
115I’ll have a word with him.

Enter HIERONIMO and a SERVANT.

HIERONIMO

116And where’s the Duke?

SERVANT

And where’s the Duke? Yonder.

HIERONIMO

And where’s the Duke? Yonder. Even so. —
117What new device have they devisèd, trow?
118Pocas palabras! mild as the lamb!
119Is’t I will be reveng’d? No, I am not the man. —

CASTILE

120Welcome, Hieronimo.

LORENZO

121Welcome, Hieronimo.

BALTHAZAR

122Welcome, Hieronimo.

HIERONIMO

123My lords, I thank you for Horatio.

CASTILE

124Hieronimo, the reason that I sent
125To speak with you, is this.

HIERONIMO

To speak with you, is this. What, so short?
126Then I’ll be gone. I thank you for’t.

CASTILE

127Nay, stay, Hieronimo! —go, call him, son.

LORENZO

128Hieronimo, my father craves a word with you.

HIERONIMO

129With me, sir? Why, my lord, I thought you had done.

LORENZO

130[aside.] No; Would he had!aparte

CASTILE

[aside.] No; Would he had! Hieronimo, I hear
131You find yourself aggrievèd at my son,
132Because you have not access unto the King;
133And say ’tis he that intercepts your suits.

HIERONIMO

134Why, is not this a miserable thing, my lord?

CASTILE

135Hieronimo, I hope you have no cause,
136And would be loath that one of your deserts
137Should once have reason to suspect my son,
138Considering how I think of you myself.

HIERONIMO

139Your son Lorenzo! whom, my noble lord?
140The hope of Spain, mine honourable friend?
141Grant me the combat of them, if they dare:

Draws out his sword.

142I’ll meet him face to face to tell me so!
143These be the scandalous reports of such
144As loves not me, and hate my lord too much:
145Should I suspect Lorenzo would prevent
146Or cross my suit, that loved my son so well?
147My lord, I am asham’d it should be said.

LORENZO

148Hieronimo, I never gave you cause.

HIERONIMO

149My good lord, I know you did not.

CASTILE

150There then pause;
151And for the satisfaction of the world,
152Hieronimo, frequent my homely house,
153The Duke of Castile, Cyprian’s ancient seat;
154And when thou wilt, use me, my son and it:
155But here, before Prince Balthazar and me,
156Embrace each other, and be perfect friends.

HIERONIMO

157Ay, marry, my lord, and shall.
158Friends, quoth he? see, I’ll be friends with you all:
159Especially with you, my lovely lord;
160For divers causes it is fit for us
161That we be friends: the world is suspicious,
162And men may think what we imagine not.

BALTHAZAR

163Why, this is friendly done, Hieronimo.

LORENZO

164And thus, I hope, old grudges are forgot.

HIERONIMO

165What else? it were a shame it should not be so.

CASTILE

166Come on, Hieronimo, at my request;
167Let us entreat your company to-day.

Exeunt.

HIERONIMO

168Your lordship’s to command. — Pah! keep your way:
169Chi mi fa più carezze che non suole,

Exit.

170Tradito mi ha, o tradir vuole.

[SCENE XV]

GHOST and REVENGE

GHOST

1Awake, Erichtho! Cerberus, awake!
2Solicit Pluto, gentle Proserpine!
3To combat, Acheron and Erebus!
4For ne’er by Styx and Phlegethon, in hell
5[Was I distress’d with outrage sore as this,]
6Nor ferried Charon to the fiery lakes
7Such fearful sights, as poor Andrea sees!
8Revenge, awake!

REVENGE

Revenge, awake! Awake? For why?

GHOST

9Awake, Revenge; for thou art ill-advis’d
10To sleep —awake! What, thou art warn’d to watch!

REVENGE

11Content thyself, and do not trouble me.

GHOST

12Awake, Revenge, if love —as love hath had —
13Have yet the power or prevalence in hell!
14Hieronimo with Lorenzo is join’d in league,
15And intercepts our passage to revenge:
16Awake, Revenge, or we are woe-begone!

REVENGE

17Thus worldlings ground, what they have dream’d upon.
18Content thyself, Andrea: though I sleep,
19Yet is my mood soliciting their souls.
20Sufficeth thee that poor Hieronimo
21Cannot forget his son Horatio.
22Nor dies Revenge, although he sleep awhile;
23For in unquiet, quietness is feign’d,
24And slumb’ring is a common worldly wile.
25Behold, Andrea, for an instance, how
26Revenge hath slept, and then imagine thou,
27What ’tis to be subject to destiny.

Enter a Dumb Show.

GHOST

28Awake, Revenge; reveal this mystery.

REVENGE

29[Lo!] the two first the nuptial torches bore
30As brightly burning as the mid-day’s sun;
31But after them doth Hymen hie as fast,
32Clothèd in sable and a saffron robe,
33And blows them out, and quencheth them with blood,
34As discontent that things continue so.

GHOST

35Sufficeth me; thy meaning’s understood,
36And thanks to thee and those infernal powers,
37That will not tolerate a lover’s woe.
38Rest thee, for I will sit to see the rest.

REVENGE

39Then argue not, for thou hast thy request.

Act IV

[SCENE I]

Enter BEL-IMPERIA and HIERONIMO.

BEL-IMPERIA

1Is this the love thou bear’st Horatio?
2Is this the kindness that thou counterfeits?
3Are these the fruits of thine incessant tears?
4Hieronimo, are these thy passions,
5Thy protestations and thy deep laments,
6That thou wert wont to weary men withal?
7O unkind father! O deceitful world!
8With what excuses canst thou show thyself
9From this dishonour and the hate of men?
10Thus to neglect the loss and life of him
11Whom both my letters and thine own belief
12Assures thee to be causeless slaughtered!
13Hieronimo, for shame, Hieronimo,
14Be not a history to after-times
15Of such ingratitude unto thy son:
16Unhappy mothers of such children then,
17But monstrous fathers to forget so soon
18The death of those, whom they, with care and cost
19Have tender’d so, thus careless should be lost.
20Myself, a stranger in respect of thee,
21So lov’d his life, as still I wish their deaths.
22Nor shall his death be unreveng’d by me,
23Although I bear it out for fashion’s sake:
24For here I swear, in sight of heaven and earth,
25Shouldst thou neglect the love thou shouldst retain,
26And give it over, and devise no more,
27Myself should send their hateful souls to hell,
28That wrought his downfall with extremest death.

HIERONIMO

29But may it be that Bel-imperia
30Vows such revenge as she hath deign’d to say?
31Why, then I see that heaven applies our drift,
32And all the saints do sit soliciting
33For vengeance on those cursèd murderers.
34Madam, ’tis true, and now I find it so,
35I found a letter, written in your name,
36And in that letter, how Horatio died.
37Pardon, O pardon, Bel-imperia,
38My fear and care in not believing it;
39Nor think I thoughtless think upon a mean
40To let his death be unreveng’d at full.
41And here I vow —so you but give consent,
42And will conceal my resolution —
43I will ere long determine of their deaths
44That causeless thus have murderèd my son.

BEL-IMPERIA

45Hieronimo, I will consent, conceal,
46And aught that may effect for thine avail,
47Join with thee to revenge Horatio’s death.

HIERONIMO

48On, then; whatsoever I devise,
49Let me entreat you, grace my practices,
50For why the plot’s already in mine head.
51Here they are.

Enter BALTHAZAR and LORENZO.

BALTHAZAR

Here they are. How now, Hieronimo?
52What, courting Bel-imperia?

HIERONIMO

What, courting Bel-imperia? Ay, my lord;
53Such courting as (I promise you)
54She hath my heart; but you, my lord, have hers.

LORENZO

55But now, Hieronimo, or never,
56We are to entreat your help.

HIERONIMO

We are to entreat your help. My help?
57Why, my good lords, assure yourselves of me;
58For you have giv’n me cause,
59Ay, by my faith, have you!

BALTHAZAR

Ay, by my faith, have you! It pleas’d you,
60At the entertainment of the ambassador,
61To grace the King so much as with a show.
62Now, were your study so well furnished,
63As for the passing of the first night’s sport
64To entertain my father with the like,
65Or any such-like pleasing motion,
66Assure yourself, it would content them well.

HIERONIMO

67Is this all?

BALTHAZAR

Is this all? Ay, this is all.

HIERONIMO

68Why then, I’ll fit you: say no more.
69When I was young, I gave my mind
70And plied myself to fruitless poetry;
71Which though it profit the professor naught,
72Yet is it passing pleasing to the world.

LORENZO

73And how for that?

HIERONIMO

And how for that? Marry, my good lord, thus:
74(And yet methinks you are too quick with us)
75When in Toledo there I studièd,
76It was my chance to write a tragedy:
77See here, my lords –

He shows them a book.

78Which, long forgot, I found this other day.
79Now would your lordships favour me so much
80As but to grace me with your acting it —
81I mean each one of you to play a part —
82Assure you it will prove most passing strange,
83And wondrous plausible to that assembly.

BALTHAZAR

84What, would you have us play a tragedy?

HIERONIMO

85Why, Nero thought it no disparagement,
86And kings and emperors have ta’en delight
87To make experience of their wits in plays.

LORENZO

88Nay, be not angry, good Hieronimo;
89The Prince but ask’d a question.

BALTHAZAR

90In faith, Hieronimo, an you be in earnest,
91I’ll make one.

LORENZO

I’ll make one. And I another.

HIERONIMO

92Now, my good lord, could you entreat
93Your sister Bel-imperia to make one?
94For what’s a play without a woman in it?

BEL-IMPERIA

95Little entreaty shall serve me, Hieronimo;
96For I must needs be employèd in your play.

HIERONIMO

97Why, this is well: I tell you, lordings,
98It was determinèd to have been acted,
99By gentlemen and scholars too,
100Such as could tell what to speak.

BALTHAZAR

101And now it shall be play’d by princes and courtiers,
102Such as can tell how to speak:
103If, as it is our country manner,
104You will but let us know the argument.

HIERONIMO

105That shall I roundly. The chronicles of Spain
106Record this written of a knight of Rhodes:
107He was betroth’d and wedded at the length,
108To one Perseda, an Italian dame,
109Whose beauty ravish’d all that her beheld,
110Especially the soul of Soliman,
111Who at the marriage was the chiefest guest.
112By sundry means sought Soliman to win
113Perseda’s love, and could not gain the same.
114Then ‘gan he break his passions to a friend,
115One of his bashaws, whom he held full dear;
116Her had this bashaw long solicited,
117And saw she was not otherwise to be won,
118But by her husband’s death, this knight of Rhodes,
119Whom presently by treachery he slew.
120She, stirr’d with an exceeding hate therefor,
121As cause of this slew Soliman,
122And, to escape the bashaw’s tyranny.
123Did stab herself: and this the tragedy.

LORENZO

124Oh, excellent!

BEL-IMPERIA

Oh, excellent! But say, Hieronimo,
125What then became of him that was the bashaw?

HIERONIMO

126Marry, thus: mov’d with remorse of his misdeeds,
127Ran to a mountain-top and hung himself.

BALTHAZAR

128But which of us is to perform that part?

HIERONIMO

129O, that will I, my lords; make no doubt of it:
130I’ll play the murderer, I warrant you,
131For I already have conceited that.

BALTHAZAR

132And what shall I?

HIERONIMO

133Great Suleiman, the Turkish emperor.

LORENZO

134And I?

HIERONIMO

And I? Erastus, the Knight of Rhodes.

BEL-IMPERIA

135And I?

HIERONIMO

And I? Perseda, chaste and resolute. —
136And here, my lords, are several abstracts drawn,
137For each of you to note your parts,
138And act it, as occasion’s offer’d you.
139You must provide [you with] a Turkish cap,
140A black mustachio and a falchion;

Gives a paper to Balthazar.

141You with a cross, like to a knight of Rhodes;

Gives another to Lorenzo.

142And, madam, you must attire yourself

He giveth Bel-imperia another.

143Like Phoebe, Flora, or the Huntress,
144Which to your discretion shall seem best.
145And as for me, my lords, I’ll look to one,
146And with the ransom that the Viceroy sent,
147So furnish and perform this tragedy,
148As all the world shall say, Hieronimo
149Was liberal in gracing of it so.

BALTHAZAR

150Hieronimo, methinks a comedy were better.

HIERONIMO

151A comedy?
152Fie! comedies are fit for common wits:
153But to present a kingly troop withal,
154Give me a stately-written tragedy;
155Tragedia cothurnata, fitting kings,
156Containing matter, and not common things.
157My lords, all this must be perform’d
158As fitting for the first night’s revelling.
159The Italian tragedians were so sharp of wit,
160That in one hour’s meditation
161They would perform anything in action.

LORENZO

162And well it may; for I have seen the like
163In Paris ’mongst the French tragedians.

HIERONIMO

164In Paris? mass, and well rememberèd!
165There’s one thing more that rests for us to do.

BALTHAZAR

166What’s that, Hieronimo? Forget not anything.

HIERONIMO

167Each one of us
168Must act his part in unknown languages,
169That it may breed the more variety:
170As you, my lord, in Latin, I in Greek,
171You in Italian, and for because I know
172That Bel-imperia hath practis’d the French,
173In courtly French shall all her phrases be.

BEL-IMPERIA

174You mean to try my cunning, then, Hieronimo?

BALTHAZAR

175But this will be a mere confusion,
176And hardly shall we all be understood.

HIERONIMO

177It must be so, for the conclusion
178Shall prove the invention and all was good:
179And I myself in an oration,
180And with a strange and wondrous show besides,
181That I will have there behind a curtain,
182Assure yourself, shall make the matter known:
183And all shall be concluded in one scene,
184For there’s no pleasure ta’en in tediousness.

BALTHAZAR

185How like you this?

LORENZO

How like you this? Why, thus, my lord:
186We must resolve to soothe his humours up.

BALTHAZAR

187On, then, Hieronimo; Farewell till soon.

HIERONIMO

188You’ll ply this gear?

LORENZO

You’ll ply this gear? I warrant you.

Exeunt all but Hieronimo.

HIERONIMO

You’ll ply this gear? I warrant you. Why so:
189Now shall I see the fall of Babylon,
190Wrought by the heav’ns in this confusion.
191And if the world like not this tragedy,
192Hard is the hap of old Hieronimo.

Exit.

[SCENE II]

Enter ISABELLA with a weapon.

ISABELLA

1Tell me no more! —O monstrous homicides!
2Since neither piety nor pity moves
3The King to justice or compassion,
4I will revenge myself upon this place,
5Where thus they murder’d my belovèd son.

She cuts down the arbour.

6Down with these branches and these loathsome boughs
7Of this unfortunate and fatal pine:
8Down with them, Isabella; rend them up,
9And burn the roots from whence the rest is sprung.
10I will not leave a root, a stalk, a tree,
11A bough, a branch, a blossom, nor a leaf,
12No, not an herb within this garden-plot —
13Accursèd complot of my misery!
14Fruitless for ever may this garden be,
15Barren the earth, and blissless whosoe’er
16Imagines not to keep it unmanur’d!
17An eastern wind commix’d with noisome airs,
18Shall blast the plants and the young saplings;
19The earth with serpents shall be pester’d,
20And passengers, for fear to be infect,
21Shall stand aloof, and, looking at it, tell:
22“There, murder’d, died the son of Isabel.”
23Ay, here he died, and here I him embrace:
24See, where his ghost solicits, with his wounds,
25Revenge on her that should revenge his death.
26Hieronimo, make haste to see thy son;
27For sorrow and despair hath cited me
28To hear Horatio plead with Rhadamanth:
29Make haste, Hieronimo, to hold excus’d
30Thy negligence in pursuit of their deaths
31Whose hateful wrath bereav’d him of his breath. —
32Ah, nay, thou dost delay their deaths,
33Forgives the murderers of thy noble son,
34And none but I bestir me—to no end!
35And as I curse this tree from further fruit,
36So shall my womb be cursèd for his sake,
37And with this weapon will I wound the breast,
38The hapless breast, that gave Horatio suck.

She stabs herself.[Exit]

[SCENE III.]

Enter HIERONIMO; he knocks up the curtain.

Enter the Duke of CASTILE.

CASTILE

1How now, Hieronimo, where’s your fellows,
2That you take all this pain?

HIERONIMO

3O sir, it is for the author’s credit,
4To look that all things may go well.
5But, good my lord, let me entreat your grace
6To give the King the copy of the play:
7This is the argument of what we show.

CASTILE

8I will, Hieronimo.

HIERONIMO

I will, Hieronimo. One thing more, my good lord.

CASTILE

9What’s that?

HIERONIMO

What’s that? Let me entreat your grace
10That, when the train are pass’d into the gallery,
11You would vouchsafe to throw me down the key.

CASTILE

12I will, Hieronimo.

Exit Castile.

HIERONIMO

13What, are you ready, Balthazar?
14Bring a chair and a cushion for the King.

Enter BALTHAZAR, with a chair.

15Well done, Balthazar! Hang up the title:
16Our scene is Rhodes; —what, is your beard on?

BALTHAZAR

17Half on; the other is in my hand.

HIERONIMO

18Despatch, for shame, are you so long?

Exit Balthazar.

19Bethink thyself, Hieronimo,
20Recall thy wits, recount thy former wrongs
21Thou hast receiv’d by murder of thy son,
22And lastly, not least, how Isabel,
23Once his mother and thy dearest wife,
24All woe-begone for him, hath slain herself.
25Behoves thee then, Hieronimo, to be reveng’d:
26The plot is laid of dire revenge:
27On then, Hieronimo, pursue revenge,
28For nothing wants but acting of revenge.

Exit Hieronimo.

[SCENE IV.]

Enter Spanish KING, VICEROY, the Duke of CASTILE, and their train.

KING

1Now, Viceroy, shall we see the tragedy
2Of Soliman, the Turkish emperor,
3Perform’d of pleasure by your son the prince,
4My nephew Don Lorenzo, and my niece.

VICEROY

5Who? Bel-imperia?

KING

6Ay, and Hieronimo, our marshal,
7At whose request they deign to do’t themselves:
8These be our pastimes in the court of Spain.
9Here, brother, you shall be the book-keeper:
10This is the argument of that they show.

He giveth him a book.

Gentlemen, this play of Hieronimo, in sundry languages, was thought good to be set down in English more largely, for the easier understanding to every public reader.

Enter BALTHAZAR, BEL-IMPERIA, and HIERONIMO.

BALTHAZAR

11Bashaw, that Rhodes is ours, yield heavens the honour,
12And holy Mahomet, our sacred prophet!
13And be thou grac’d with every excellence
14That Soliman can give, or thou desire.
15But thy desert in conquering Rhodes is less
16Than in reserving this fair Christian nymph,
17Perseda, blissful lamp of excellence,
18Whose eyes compel, like powerful adamant,
19The warlike heart of Suleiman to wait.

KING

20See, Viceroy, that is Balthazar, your son,
21That represents the emperor Soliman:
22How well he acts his amorous passion!

VICEROY

23Ay, Bel-imperia hath taught him that.

CASTILE

24That’s because his mind runs all on Bel-imperia.

HIERONIMO

25Whatever joy earth yields betide your majesty.

BALTHAZAR

26Earth yields no joy without Perseda’s love.

HIERONIMO

27Let then Perseda on your grace attend.

BALTHAZAR

28She shall not wait on me, but I on her:
29Drawn by the influence of her lights, I yield.
30But let my friend, the Rhodian knight, come forth,
31Erasto, dearer than my life to me,
32That he may see Perseda, my belov’d.

Enter [LORENZO as] Erasto.

KING

33Here comes Lorenzo: look upon the plot,
34And tell me, brother, what part plays he?

BEL-IMPERIA

35Ah, my Erasto, welcome to Perseda.

LORENZO

36Thrice happy is Erasto that thou liv’st;
37Rhodes’ loss is nothing to Erasto’s joy:
38Sith his Perseda lives, his life survives.

BALTHAZAR

39Ah, bashaw, here is love between Erasto
40And fair Perseda, sovereign of my soul.

HIERONIMO

41Remove Erasto, mighty Soliman,
42And then Perseda will be quickly won.

BALTHAZAR

43Erasto is my friend; and while he lives,
44Perseda never will remove her love.

HIERONIMO

45Let not Erasto live to grieve great Soliman.

BALTHAZAR

46Dear is Erasto in our princely eye.

HIERONIMO

47But if he be your rival, let him die.

BALTHAZAR

48Why, let him die! —so love commandeth me.
49Yet grieve I that Erasto should so die.

HIERONIMO

50Erasto, Soliman saluteth thee,
51And lets thee wit by me his highness’ will,
52Which is, thou shouldst be thus employ’d.

Stabs him.

BEL-IMPERIA

Which is, thou shouldst be thus employ’d. Ay me!
53Erasto! see, Soliman, Erasto’s slain!

BALTHAZAR

54Yet liveth Soliman to comfort thee.
55Fair queen of beauty, let not favour die,
56But with a gracious eye behold his grief,
57That with Perseda’s beauty is increas’d
58If by Perseda grief be not releas’d.

BEL-IMPERIA

59Tyrant, desist soliciting vain suits;
60Relentless are mine ears to thy laments,
61As thy butcher is pitiless and base,
62Which seiz’d on my Erasto, harmless knight.
63Yet by thy power thou thinkest to command,
64And to thy power Perseda doth obey:
65But, were she able, thus she would revenge
66Thy treacheries on thee, ignoble Prince:

Stabs him.

67And on herself she would be thus reveng’d.

Stabs herself.

KING

68Well said, old Marshal, this was bravely done!

HIERONIMO

69But Bel-imperia plays Perseda well!

VICEROY

70Were this in earnest, Bel-imperia,
71You would be better to my son than so.

KING

72But now what follows for Hieronimo?

HIERONIMO

73Marry, this follows for Hieronimo:
74Here break we off our sundry languages,
75And thus conclude I in our vulgar tongue.
76Haply you think —but bootless are your thoughts —
77That this is fabulously counterfeit,
78And that we do as all tragedians do:
79To die to-day (for fashioning our scene)
80The death of Ajax, or some Roman peer,
81And in a minute starting up again,
82Revive to please to-morrow’s audience.
83No, princes; know I am Hieronimo,
84The hopeless father of a hapless son,
85Whose tongue is tun’d to tell his latest tale,
86Not to excuse gross errors in the play.
87I see your looks urge instance of these words;
88Behold the reason urging me to this:

Shows his dead son.

89See here my show, look on this spectacle:
90Here lay my hope, and here my hope hath end;
91Here lay my heart, and here my heart was slain;
92Here lay my treasure, here my treasure lost;
93Here lay my bliss, and here my bliss bereft:
94But hope, heart, treasure, joy and bliss,
95All fled, fail’d, died, yea, all decay’d with this.
96From forth these wounds came breath that gave me life;
97They murder’d me that made these fatal marks.
98The cause was love, whence grew this mortal hate;
99The hate, Lorenzo and young Balthazar;
100The love, my son to Bel-imperia.
101But night, the coverer of accursèd crimes,
102With pitchy silence hush’d these traitors’ harms,
103And lent them leave, for they had sorted leisure
104To take advantage in my garden-plot
105Upon my son, my dear Horatio:
106There merciless, they butcher’d up my boy,
107In black, dark night, to pale, dim, cruel death.
108He shrieks: I heard (and yet, methinks, I hear)
109His dismal outcry echo in the air.
110With soonest speed I hasted to the noise,
111Where hanging on a tree I found my son,
112Through-girt with wounds, and slaughter’d as you see.
113And griev’d I, think you, at this spectacle?
114Speak, Portuguese, whose loss resembles mine:
115If thou canst weep upon thy Balthazar,
116’Tis like I wail’d for my Horatio.
117And you, my lord, whose reconcilèd son
118March’d in a net, and thought himself unseen,
119And rated me for brainsick lunacy,
120With “God amend that mad Hieronimo” —
121How can you brook our play’s catastrophe?
122And here behold this bloody handkercher,
123Which at Horatio’s death I weeping dipp’d
124Within the river of his bleeding wounds:
125It as propitious, see, I have reserv’d,
126And never hath it left my bloody heart,
127Soliciting remembrance of my vow
128With these, O, these accurs’d murderers:
129Which now perform’d, my heart is satisfied.
130And to this end the bashaw I became
131That might revenge me on Lorenzo’s life,
132Who therefore was appointed to the part,
133And was to represent the Knight of Rhodes,
134That I might kill him more conveniently.
135So, Viceroy, was this Balthazar, thy son,
136That Soliman which Bel-imperia,
137In person of Perseda murderèd,
138Solely appointed to that tragic part
139That she might slay him that offended her.
140Poor Bel-imperia miss’d her part in this:
141For though the story saith she should have died,
142Yet I of kindness and of care to her,
143Did otherwise determine of her end;
144But love of him whom they did hate too much
145Did urge her resolution to be such. —
146And, princes, now behold Hieronimo,
147Author and actor in this tragedy,
148Bearing his latest fortune in his fist;
149And will as resolute conclude his part,
150As any of the actors gone before.
151And, gentles, thus I end my play;
152Urge no more words: I have no more to say.

He runs to hang himself.

KING

153O hearken, Viceroy! Hold, Hieronimo!
154Brother, my nephew and thy son are slain!

VICEROY

155We are betray’d; My Balthazar is slain!
156Break ope the doors; run, save Hieronimo!

[They break in and hold Hieronimo.]

157Hieronimo,
158Do but inform the King of these events;
159Upon mine honour, thou shalt have no harm.

HIERONIMO

160Viceroy, I will not trust thee with my life,
161Which I this day have offer’d to my son.
162Accursèd wretch!
163Why stay’st thou him that was resolv’d to die?

KING

164Speak, traitor! damned, bloody murderer, speak!
165For now I have thee, I will make thee speak.
166Why hast thou done this undeserving deed?

VICEROY

167Why hast thou murderèd my Balthazar?

CASTILE

168Why hast thou butcher’d both my children thus?

HIERONIMO

169§ Oh, good words!
170As dear to me was my Horatio,
171As yours, or yours, or yours, my lord, to you.
172My guiltless son was by Lorenzo slain,
173And by Lorenzo and that Balthazar
174Am I at last revenged thoroughly,
175Upon whose souls may heavens be yet avenged
176With greater far than these afflictions.

CASTILE

177But who were thy confederates in this?

VICEROY

178That was thy daughter Bel-imperia,
179For by her hand my Balthazar was slain.
180I saw her stab him.

KING

181Why speak’st thou not?

HIERONIMO

182What lesser liberty can kings afford
183Than harmless silence? Then afford it me.
184Sufficeth I may not, nor I will not, tell thee.

KING

185Fetch forth the tortures! —Traitor as thou art,
186I’ll make thee tell.

HIERONIMO

I’ll make thee tell. Indeed
187Thou mayst torment me as his wretched son
188Hath done in murdering my Horatio.
189But never shalt thou force me to reveal
190The thing which I have vowed inviolate.
191And therefore, in despite of all thy threats,
192Pleased with their deaths, and eased with their revenge,
193First take my tongue and afterwards my heart. §
194<sup> Q4</sup> But are you sure they are dead?

CASTILE

<sup> Q4</sup> But are you sure they are dead? Ay, slave, too sure.

HIERONIMO

195What, and yours too?

VICEROY

196Ay, all are dead; not one of them survive.

HIERONIMO

197Nay, then I care not; come, and we shall be friends,
198Let us lay our heads together.
199See, here’s a goodly noose will hold them all.

VICEROY

200O damnèd devil, how secure he is!

HIERONIMO

201Secure? Why, dost thou wonder at it?
202I tell thee, Viceroy, this day I have seen revenge,
203And in that sight am grown a prouder monarch,
204Than ever sat under the crown of Spain.
205Had I as many lives as there be stars,
206As many heavens to go, to as those lives,
207I’d give them all, ay, and my soul to boot,
208But I would see thee ride in this red pool.

CASTILE

209Speak! Who were thy confederates in this?

VICEROY

210That was thy daughter Bel-imperia,
211For by her hand my Balthazar was slain.
212I saw her stab him.

HIERONIMO

213Oh, good words!
214As dear to me was my Horatio,
215As yours, or yours, or yours, my lord, to you.
216My guiltless son was by Lorenzo slain,
217And by Lorenzo and that Balthazar
218Am I at last reveng’d thoroughly,
219Upon whose souls may heavens be yet aveng’d
220With greater far than these afflictions.
221Methinks since I grew inward with revenge,
222I cannot look with scorn enough on death.

KING

223What, dost thou mock us, slave? bring tortures forth.

HIERONIMO

224Do, do, do: and meantime I’ll torture you.
225You had a son, as I take it; and your son
226Should ha’ been married to your daughter:
227Ha, was’t not so? —You had a son too,
228He was my liege’s nephew, he was proud
229And politic; had he liv’d, he might have come
230To wear the crown of Spain (I think ’twas so):
231’Twas I that kill’d him; look you, this same hand,
232’Twas it that stabb’d his heart — do you see this hand?
233For one Horatio, if you ever knew him: a youth,
234One that they hang’d up in his father’s garden:
235One that did force your valiant son to yield,
236While your more valiant son did take him prisoner.

VICEROY

237Be deaf, my senses; I can hear no more.

KING

238Fall, heav’n, and cover us with thy sad ruins.

CASTILE

239Roll all the world within thy pitchy cloud.

HIERONIMO

240Now do I applaud what I have acted.
241Nunc iners cadat manus!
242Now to express the rupture of my part,
243First take my tongue, and afterward my heart. </sup> Q4 <sup>

[He bites out his tongue.]

KING

244O monstrous resolution of a wretch!
245See, Viceroy, he hath bitten forth his tongue,
246Rather than to reveal what we requir’d.

CASTILE

247Yet can he write.

KING

248And if in this he satisfy us not,
249We will devise th’ extremest kind of death
250That ever was invented for a wretch.

Then he makes signs for a knife to mend his pen.

CASTILE

251O he would have a knife to mend his pen.

VICEROY

252Here, and advise thee that thou write the troth.

KING

253Look to my brother! Save Hieronimo!

Hieronimo with a knife stabs the duke and himself.

254What age hath ever heard such monstrous deeds?
255My brother, and the whole succeeding hope
256That Spain expected after my decease! —
257Go, bear his body hence, that we may mourn
258The loss of our belovèd brother’s death,
259That he may be entomb’d whate’er befall;
260I am the next, the nearest, last of all.

VICEROY

261And thou, Don Pedro, do the like for us:
262Take up our hapless son, untimely slain;
263Set me with him, and he with woeful me,
264Upon the main-mast of a ship unmann’d,
265And let the wind and tide haul me along
266To Scylla’s barking and untamèd gulf,
267Or to the loathsome pool of Acheron,
268To weep my want for my sweet Balthazar:
269Spain hath no refuge for a Portingale.

The trumpets sound a dead march; the King of Spain

270mourning after his brother’s body, and the King of
271Portingale bearing the body of his son. [Exeunt.]

[SCENE V.]

GHOST and REVENGE.

GHOST

1Ay, now my hopes have end in their effects,
2When blood and sorrow finish my desires:
3Horatio murder’d in his father’s bower,
4Vile Serberine by Pedringano slain;
5False Pedringano hang’d by quaint device;
6Fair Isabella by herself misdone;
7Prince Balthazar by Bel-imperia stabb’d;
8The Duke of Castile and his wicked son
9Both done to death by old Hieronimo;
10My Bel-imperia fall’n as Dido fell,
11And good Hieronimo slain by himself:
12Ay, these were spectacles to please my soul! —
13Now will I beg at lovely Proserpine
14That, by the virtue of her princely doom,
15I may consort my friends in pleasing sort,
16And on my foes work just and sharp revenge.
17I’ll lead my friend Horatio through those fields,
18Where never-dying wars are still inur’d;
19I’ll lead fair Isabella to that train,
20Where pity weeps, but never feeleth pain;
21I’ll lead my Bel-imperia to those joys,
22That vestal virgins and fair queens possess;
23I’ll lead Hieronimo where Orpheus plays,
24Adding sweet pleasure to eternal days.
25But say, Revenge —for thou must help, or none —
26Against the rest how shall my hate be shown?

REVENGE

27This hand shall hale them down to deepest hell
28Where none but Furies, bugs and tortures dwell.

GHOST

29Then, sweet Revenge, do this at my request:
30Let me be judge, and doom them to unrest.
31Let loose poor Tityus from the vulture’s gripe,
32And let Don Cyprian supply his room;
33Place Don Lorenzo on Ixion’s wheel,
34And let the lover’s endless pains surcease
35(Juno forgets old wrath, and grants him ease);
36Hang Balthazar about Chimaera’s neck,
37And let him there bewail his bloody love,
38Repining at our joys that are above;
39Let Serberine go roll the fatal stone,
40And take from Sisyphus his endless moan;
41False Pedringano, for his treachery,
42Let him be dragg’d through boiling Acheron,
43And there live, dying still in endless flames,
44Blaspheming gods and all their holy names.

REVENGE

45Then haste we down to meet thy friends and foes:
46To place thy friends in ease, the rest in woes;
47For here though death hath end their misery,
48I’ll there begin their endless tragedy.

Exeunt.

La tragedia española

Thomas Kyd — EMOTHE0307_LaTragediaEspanola

PERSONAJES

  • ESPECTRO de Andrés, noble español, coro
  • VENGANZA, coro
  • REY de España
  • Cipriano, DUQUE DE CASTILLA, su hermano
  • LORENZO, hijo del Duque
  • BEL-IMPERIA, hermana de Lorenzo
  • VIRREY de Portugal
  • BALTASAR, su hijo
  • DON PEDRO, hermano del Virrey
  • JERÓNIMO, Justicia Mayor de España
  • ISABELA, su esposa
  • HORACIO, su hijo
  • GENERAL español
  • ALGUACIL
  • Don BAZULTO/SENEX/VIEJO, viejo
  • Tres CIUDADANOS
  • EMBAJADOR Portugués
  • ALEJANDRO, Noble portugués
  • VILLUPO, Noble portugués
  • NOBLE en la corte portuguesa
  • Dos portugueses
  • PEDRINGANO, Criado de Bel-Imperia
  • CRISTÓFILO, Custodio de Bel-Imperia
  • PAJE de Lorenzo
  • SERBERINO, Criado de Baltasar
  • DONCELLA de Isabela
  • MENSAJERO
  • VERDUGO
  • Tres reyes y tres caballeros de la primera pantomima
  • Himeneo y tres portadores de antorchas de la segunda pantomima
  • BAZARDO, pintor
  • PEDRO, criado de Jerónimo
  • DIEGO, criado de Jerónimo
  • CRIADO de Jerónimo
  • Tres vigilantes
  • Un ejército. Nobles. Alabarderos. Oficiales. Trompetas. Criados
  • PRIMER CIUDADANO
  • SEGUNDO CIUDADANO
  • TERCER CIUDADANO
  • PRIMER VIGILANTE
  • SEGUNDO VIGILANTE
  • TERCER VIGILANTE
  • PINTOR
  • ANDRÉS, Espectro de Andrés
  • Criado de Jerónimo
  • Criado del duque de Castilla
  • MUCHACHO, Otra denominacion par el paje de Lorenzo

[ACTO I, ESCENA I]

Salen el Espectro de Andrés y, con él, la Venganza.

ESPECTRO.

1Cuando esta eterna sustancia de mi alma
2Vivía presa en mi carne sensual,
3Sirviéndose entrambas mutuamente,
4Fui un cortesano en España.
5Mi nombre era Andrés y mi ascendencia,
6Si bien no innoble, era inferior en mucho
7A la feliz fortuna de mi juventud;
8Pues entonces, en el cénit de mi edad,
9Por mi fiel servicio y el merecimiento
10De mi amor, en secreto, tuve el gozo
11De poseer a una noble dama,
12Por dulce nombre llamada Bel-Imperia.
13Pero en la feliz recolección
14De mis preciados gozos estivales
15El invierno de la muerte marchitó
16La flor y el fruto de este mi deleite,
17Forzando el divorcio entre mi amor y yo.
18Porque en la última guerra portuguesa
19El valor me arrastró hasta la boca
20Del peligro y allí encontró la muerte
21Pasaje a través de mis heridas.
22Cuando morí, bajó mi alma al punto
23A vadear el caudaloso río
24Del Aquerón; mas una vez allí
25Caronte, hosco y único barquero,
26Declaró que, no habiéndose cumplido
27Con mis debidos ritos funerales,
28No podría ir yo entre sus pasajeros.
29No había el Sol dormido ni tres noches
30En el regazo de Tetis, ni había
31Templado en su mar el humeante carro
32Cuando mis funerales y exequias
33Devotamente Don Horacio oficia,
34El hijo de nuestro Justicia.
35Se avino entonces el infernal barquero
36A transportarme a la lodosa orilla
37Que conduce a las ondas del Averno.
38Allí, complaciendo con discurso
39Almibarado al fiero Cancerbero,
40Los peligros pasé de los vestíbulos
41Más externos del infernal recinto.
42Y no lejos de allí, entre diez mil almas,
43Minos se sentaba, y Éaco, y Radamanto;
44A los cuales, apenas me aproximo
45Para implorar pasaje a mi alma errante,
46Cuando Minos, de hojas en que escrito
47Estaba el albur de mi destino,
48Extrae el modo de mi vida y muerte.
49“Este hidalgo”, sentencia, “enamorado
50Vivió y murió, y por su amor probó
51Los lances y fortuna de la guerra,
52Y a la fortuna y lances de la guerra
53Rindió tanto su amor como su vida”.
54“Así pues”, dice Éaco, “de aquí llevadlo
55A andar en nuestro prado entre amadores
56Y allí a pasar el tiempo eternamente
57A la sombra del mirto y del ciprés”.
58“Mas no, no ha de ser”, dice Radamanto,
59“Mezclar soldados con amantes almas:
60Murió en la guerra, e irá a marciales campos,
61En donde herido Héctor languidece
62Y baten el terreno eternamente
63De Aquiles los fieles mirmidones”.
64Entonces Minos, el más templado juez
65De los tres, recurrió a este expediente
66Para finalizar sus diferencias:
67“Enviadlo”, dice, “a nuestro rey infernal,
68Para que su hado sea según él juzgue”.
69Y, a ese efecto, libran salvoconducto
70Conducente a la corte de Plutón.
71Entre sombras de noche sempiterna,
72Vi más visiones de las que pudieran
73Decir mil lenguas o escribir mil plumas,
74O fraguar mil mortales corazones.
75Tres caminos había: el de la derecha
76Llevaba recto a los ya dichos campos,
77En donde amantes y soldados moran,
78Aunque cada uno en sus confines;
79El de la izquierda, en descenso horrible,
80Era caída segura hacia el infierno,
81En donde las sanguinolentas Furias
82Su látigo de duro acero agitan
83E Ixión su rueda gira eternamente;
84En donde a tragar oro fundido
85Se obliga a los viles usureros,
86Y en los lascivos se enroscan feas sierpes,
87Y con heridas que no matan nunca
88Gimen los homicidas para siempre
89Y los perjuros son allí escaldados
90Zambullidos en plomo derretido,
91Y todos los pecados execrables
92Con ingentes tormentos oprimidos.
93Por el camino que hay entrambos fui
94Y así llegué hasta el elíseo prado
95En donde se alzaba una torre altiva
96Hecha de bronce y puertas diamantinas.
97Aquí, hallando a Plutón y Proserpina,
98Muestro mi pasaporte a las deidades,
99Humilde, a sus pies arrodillado;
100Por lo cual Proserpina se sonríe,
101Y solicita poder dictar mi hado:
102Plutón lo concede complacido y sella
103Su otorgamiento con un beso.
104Tras lo cual te susurra a ti, Venganza,
105Y te ordena que rauda me conduzcas,
106Por el portal de cuerno que a los sueños
107Ofrece paso en la callada noche.
108Y apenas habla, en lo que dura un guiño,
109No sé ni cómo, aquí nos vemos ambos.

VENGANZA.

110Conoce, Andrés, entonces, que has llegado
111A dónde a quien te dio muerte verás,
112Baltasar, príncipe de Portugal,
113Sin vida a manos de Bel-Imperia.
114Sentémonos y veamos este misterio,
115Y sirvamos de coro a esta tragedia.

[ACTO I, ESCENA II]

Salen el REY DE ESPAÑA, un GENERAL, el DUQUE DE CASTILLA y JERÓNIMO.

REY.

1Decid, pues, general, ¿cómo nos va?

GENERAL.

2Muy bien, mi soberano, excepto a algunos,
3Muertos a la fortuna de la guerra.

REY.

4¿Mas qué presagia vuestra faz risueña?

GENERAL.

5Victoria, mi señor, y a bajo costo.

REY.

6¿Darán tributo, pues, nuestros portugueses?

GENERAL.

7Tributo y el homenaje acostumbrado.

REY.

8Sea entonces bendito el Dios del cielo,
9Por cuyo favor triunfa la justicia.

DUQUE DE CASTILLA.

10O multum dilecte Deo, tibi militat aether,
11Et conjuratae curvato poplite gentes
12Succumbut; recti soror est victoria juris.

REY.

13Gracias, mi amado hermano el Duque.
14Mas, General, brevemente relatad
15Vuestro orden de batalla y vuestro triunfo,
16Tal que, unido el placer de vuestras nuevas
17A la altura del anterior contento,
18Con más salario y dignidad mayor
19Podamos premiar vuestra nobleza.

GENERAL.

20Donde unen España y Portugal
21Sus lindes y se empujan mutuamente,
22Allí, soberbiamente desplegados,
23Se encontraron nuestros dos ejércitos,
24Bien equipados ambos y ambos llenos
25De esperanza y temor a iguales partes:
26Ambos amenazando con alardes,
27Ambos ondeando guiones y banderas,
28Ambos tocando cajas y trompetas,
29Ambos alzando horrísono clamor,
30Replicado por ríos, montes y valles,
31Hasta llegar al cielo con estruendo
32Que atemorizaba al cielo mismo.
33Nuestros dos batallones fueron ambos
34Dispuestos en forma de escuadrón,
35Cada extremo vallado con mosquetes;
36Pero antes que las picas se encontraran,
37Saqué un escuadrón de los más aptos
38Mosqueteros de la retaguardia
39Para iniciar la lucha con ventaja:
40Ellos hicieron avanzar entonces
41Otra ala suya a nuestro encuentro.
42Mientras tanto nuestra artillería
43Batía sus flancos y los capitanes
44Se esforzaban probando su valor.
45Don Pedro, el principal coronel
46De su caballería, intentó con su ala
47Romper nuestras filas bravamente,
48Mas don Roger, sin par hombre de armas,
49Se adelantó contra él con mosqueteros,
50Frustrando la malicia de su ataque.
51Y mientras ambos se enzarzan en refriegas
52Luchan los batallones cuerpo a cuerpo,
53Sus terribles descargas semejantes
54Al tempestuoso y rugiente océano
55Cuando, erguido en marea gigantesca,
56Se estrella en los rocosos farallones
57Y abre sus fauces cual si quisiera
58Engullir la tierra circundante.
59Entonces, mientras Belona brama,
60Densas tormentas de postas descargan
61Cual gélida granizada invernal,
62Y lanzas cimbreantes ensombrecen
63El aire turbio y perturbado.
64Pede pe et cuspide cuspis;
65Arma sonant armis, vir petiturque viro.
66Caen por cada bando capitanes,
67Y soldados, algunos malheridos,
68Otros muertos al punto en la refriega,
69Aquí un cuerpo cae descabezado,
70Allá sangrantes miembros en la hierba,
71Mezclados caballos destripados
72Y armas esparcidas por doquier.
73En esta confusión más de tres horas
74Estuvo indecisa la victoria
75Ni a una ni a otra parte inclinada,
76Hasta que Don Andrés, con sus lanceros
77Tal brecha abrió en el frente de batalla
78Que con desmayo ya cedían las huestes.
79Mas Baltasar, el joven príncipe luso,
80Trajo ayuda y animó su resistencia.
81Entonces renovóse la batalla,
82Y en la refriega muerto cayó Andrés,
83Bravo hombre de armas, mas inferior
84A Baltasar en este lance bélico.
85Pero mientras, insultando a su víctima,
86Vanagloriábase altivo el Príncipe
87Para vergüenza nuestra, la amistad
88Y el pundonor, a una coaligados,
89Incitaron a Horacio, el noble vástago
90De nuestro Justicia, a retar
91Al Príncipe en duelo singular.
92No mucho entre los dos duró la lucha,
93Pues presto el Príncipe fue desmontado
94Y forzado a rendirse y declarase
95Prisionero y rehén de su enemigo.
96Una vez fue prendido, huyeron todos,
97Perseguidos por nuestros carabinas
98Que daban muerte a los desbandados,
99Hasta que, menguando Febo hacia el Oeste,
100Se ordenó el toque de retreta.

REY.

101General, gracias, por las buenas nuevas;
